title: Latency-aware headroom estimator — experiments & notes
content:
Purpose and context:
This is a working journal for a lightweight heuristic estimator (spreadsheet + small sim) to recommend concurrency and continuous-batch headroom for production routes. Focus: give SREs and on-call/runbook owners a quick starting point to size slot counts so p95 latency objectives are unlikely to be missed under expected arrival shapes.

Quick summary (TL;DR):
- Model: approximate continuous batching as an M/G/1 queue where service time S is a function of batch size b (S(b)). Use PK formula for E[W] and a simple CV-based p95 heuristic.
- Heuristics: target utilization (rho) = 60–75% for latency-sensitive routes; choose concurrency = ceil(lambda * E[S] * 1.25) where 1.25 is an empirical headroom factor tuned from canaries.
- Batch window guidance: 8–30 ms for mixed interactive workloads, smaller (~5–10ms) for chat-style short responses; larger windows help throughput but increase p95 unless headroom increases.
- Spreadsheet layout: tab "Estimator" with inputs (arrival profile, mean tokens, per-token ms, kernel overhead), outputs (recommended concurrency, expected p50/p95, estimated GPU utilization, cost delta).

Assumptions and basic numbers used in spreadsheet (explicit so reviewers can sanity-check):
- Arrival process: baseline Poisson (good first approx) with optional burst multiplier for 1-min microbursts (x1.5–x3).
- Mean tokens per request: 80 (configurable).
- Per-token GPU time: 0.35 ms (observed on A100 quantized path for small seqs) — captured in Sheet 'Profile' A2.
- Kernel startup / amortized overhead per batch: 6 ms (includes dispatch + small kernel init + memory work).
- Effective service time S(b) = kernel_overhead + per_token_ms * tokens_in_batch + batch_merging_penalty. For simplicity tokens_in_batch approximated by request_tokens when continuous batching only merges across concurrent inflight requests; spreadsheet uses S(b) ≈ 6ms + 0.35ms * mean_tokens * b_factor where b_factor ~1 for continuous.

Queueing model and p95 approximation (notes to self):
- Using Pollaczek–Khinchine (M/G/1) to get mean waiting time E[W] = (lambda * E[S^2]) / (2 * (1 - rho)). Here rho = lambda * E[S]. We estimate E[S^2] via var(S) + E[S]^2.
- p95 heuristic: approximate tail using an exponential-like correction: p95_wait ≈ E[W] * (1 + 2 * CV_S) where CV_S = sqrt(var(S))/E[S]. This is empirical and came from comparing to small-scale sim (see linked spreadsheet).
- Total p95 latency ≈ p95_wait + S_95 (we approximate S_95 ≈ E[S] + 1.25*std(S)).
- For continuous-batching dominated service-time variability is lower (CV_S ~0.25–0.6); for multi-model fallback or variable token lengths CV_S can be >1.

Example worked numbers (play with these cells directly in sheet):
- lambda (requests/sec) = 25 r/s
- mean_tokens = 80 tokens
- per_token_ms = 0.35 ms -> service per request (no merge) ≈ 28 ms + 6 ms overhead = 34 ms -> E[S] ≈ 0.034 s
- rho per concurrency slot: with concurrency=1, rho = 25 * 0.034 = 0.85 (too high).
- recommended concurrency (base) = ceil(lambda * E[S]) = ceil(0.85) = 1 (but add headroom)
- apply heuristic headroom 1.25x -> concurrency = ceil(1 * 1.25) = 2 slots -> effective rho = 25 * 0.034 / 2 = 0.425 (good)
- E[W] approx using PK: need E[S^2]. assume std(S)=0.012 s => var=1.44e-4, E[S^2]=E[S]^2 + var = (0.034)^2 + 1.44e-4 = 1.156e-3 + 1.44e-4 = 1.3e-3 -> E[W]=(lambda*E[S^2])/(2*(1-rho_total)) where lambda=25 and rho_total=25*0.034/2=0.425 => E[W]~(25*0.0013)/(2*(1-0.425))=0.0325/(2*0.575)=0.0325/1.15=0.0283 s -> 28 ms mean wait
- p95_wait approx = E[W]*(1+2*CV_S) with CV_S=0.35 -> p95_wait ≈ 0.0283*(1+0.7)=0.0481 s (48 ms)
- total p95 ≈ 48 ms + S_95 (~0.034 + 1.25*0.012 = 0.034 + 0.015 = 0.049 s) -> p95 ≈ 97 ms.
- Interpretation: with concurrency=2 we get p95 ~97 ms for 25 r/s. If target p95 is 75 ms, bump concurrency to 3 and re-evaluate.

Continuous-batch window and its effect (operational notes):
- Window size affects batch merge factor and perceived per-request tokens_in_batch. Larger windows let more requests join same kernel run -> reduces per-token overhead but increases wait time and tail.
- In spreadsheet we model window w (ms) -> expected effective batch factor b_eff ≈ 1 + lambda * w * k where k is join efficiency (0.6–0.9). Use conservative k=0.6 for bursty routes.
- Sensitivity: doubling w increases b_eff roughly linearly and increases E[S] accordingly; however batching reduces per-request cost because kernel_overhead amortized across b_eff. Plot in sheet: "WindowSweep" tab.

Cost & utilization tradeoffs:
- Define cost per slot proportional to GPU-hours. Spreadsheet estimates cost_delta = baseline_cost * (util_target / util_current) etc. Provide quick mapping: more concurrency -> higher utilization per GPU -> lower $/request, but tail rises if headroom not increased.
- We capture steady-state savings (tokens/$) and p95 penalty. Provide an 'acceptance curve' in sheet: acceptable cost reduction threshold (e.g., must reduce cost by >10% without p95 regressions >10%).

Small sim validation and canary notes (actual runs we did):
- Ran micro-sim in sheet (Monte Carlo, 100k events) using arrival traces from PROD_ROUTE_42 (see linked artifact). Observed spreadsheet heuristic overestimates p95 by ~5–15% for lambda<=50 r/s, underestimates for heavy microburst patterns (x2 peaks) — adjust headroom to 1.4 for those.
- Canary run (staging, 24h): applied concurrency recommendation for route chat-quick-1 on dedicated cluster (concurrency 4 -> expected p95 ~120ms). Observed actual p95 135ms during a 40s microburst; root cause: model didn't include backend calls variance. TODO: add backend tail factor in S variance cell.

Operational checklist (for oncall/runbook integration):
- Inputs to edit before running estimator: arrival trace window (1m/5m), burst multiplier, per-token benchmark number (sheet 'Bench' row B2), kernel_overhead (B3).
- Run "WindowSweep" to see recommended concurrency at different windows.
- If recommended concurrency delta > 30% from current, schedule staged rollout: canary (1%), ramp to 10% over 15 min, then evaluate p95 and error-rate dashboards.
- If p95 spikes: rollback concurrency, reduce window, increase headroom.

Spreadsheet layout (IMPORTANT cells to review):
- Estimator!A2 lambda_rps (input)
- Estimator!A3 target_p95_ms (input)
- Estimator!B2 mean_tokens (input)
- Estimator!B3 per_token_ms (input)
- Estimator!B4 kernel_overhead_ms (input)
- Estimator!C2 recommended_concurrency (output, formula: =CEILING(lambda_rps*E_S*headroom))
- Estimator!C3 expected_p95_ms (output)
- WindowSweep!A1 window_ms (sweep)
- Bench!B2 microbench_token_ms (raw bench)

Open questions / TO-DOs (short running backlog):
- Replace CV-based p95 heuristic with an analytically-grounded tail bound (e.g., apply heavy-traffic large-deviation approximations) — higher-fidelity would help SLO-critical routes.
- Model multi-class traffic: low-token chat vs long generation in same queue. Current single-class model loses accuracy. Either split routes or include mixture model.
- Incorporate backend/out-of-GPU variability (external RPCs) into S variance cells and adjust headroom recommendations automatically.
- Add a damage-control guard: if simulated p99 > 2x target, auto-recommend extra conservative concurrency and smaller windows.

Notes for reviewers & where to start:
- Open the spreadsheet linked above, go to tab 'Estimator' and change lambda to match route traffic. Check 'WindowSweep' to see sensitivity.
- If you want a quick test: set mean_tokens=40 and per_token_ms=0.5 to simulate a smaller model path; see how concurrency recommendation changes.

Misc loose thoughts / scribbles
- Headroom factor seems to scale with burstiness metric B = (max_1min / mean_5min). Observational mapping: B<1.3 -> headroom 1.2; 1.3-2.0 -> headroom 1.3; >2.0 -> headroom 1.4–1.6. Put this in sheet as table.
- For routes with strict p95 < 50ms, prefer dedicated capacity with autoscale buffer; shared-hosted paths are hard to keep that tight without overprovisioning.

References and links:
- Spreadsheet: https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1A2B3C4Estimator (primary)
- Trace sample: s3://prod-traces/route-42/2026-02-18/ (anonymized)
- Jira: INF-2222 (estimator v1), INF-3344 (canary failure investigation)
- PR: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/987 (instrumentation to measure kernel_overhead)
